candidate_relations.reason: Confusion, dyspnea, hypoxia, and hypotension after a 50 m rapid ascent constitute Type II decompression sickness, the same diagnostic object as decompression sickness in this case.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Type II DCS as the neurologic/pulmonary form of decompression sickness

candidate_relations.reason: Right-heart microbubbles show gas embolism as the mechanism, not the named diagnosis of decompression sickness.
Venous gas embolism is documented in right-heart chambers and is a component of decompression sickness.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: venous gas embolism as a DCS mechanism

candidate_relations.reason: Metabolic acidosis is an ABG abnormality, not decompression sickness.
Hypoxemia and tachypnea are pulmonary manifestations of decompression sickness.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: hypoxemic respiratory failure as pulmonary DCS manifestation

candidate_relations.reason: Sepsis is not established; the context is a saturation-dive ascent.
Nitrogen embolism describes inert-gas pathophysiology of decompression sickness but is not the clinical diagnosis name.
Caisson disease is a traditional alias of decompression sickness.
Severe arthralgia is the musculoskeletal manifestation of decompression sickness.
High-pressure nervous syndrome occurs at depth, not after rapid ascent with intravascular bubbles.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: HPNS vs decompression sickness after ascent

candidate_relations.reason: No PFO was shown and bubbles were in right heart chambers, so arterial gas embolism is a related but distinct diving injury.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: arterial gas embolism vs DCS without PFO
